second_propagation_path.name: repository-gated OIDC trusted publishing
_why_this_is_the_most_important_new_TTP: Every control the corpus recommends against the primary path assumes a stolen npm
token: rotate npm credentials, gate on release age, block install scripts. This path
uses no npm token at all. It mints a real publish credential from a GitHub Actions
OIDC token, then signs the result with genuine Sigstore provenance. Provenance
verification passes because the provenance is real - which is the third time in this
campaign that attestation has proved who built an artifact rather than that it is safe.
steps: request an OIDC token with audience npm:registry.npmjs.org
trade it at npm's trusted-publishing endpoint for a real publish credential
inject the typosquatted dependency @opensearch/setup, pinned to a commit
request a second OIDC token with audience sigstore
obtain a Fulcio certificate and build SLSA v1 in-toto provenance over SHA-512
DSSE-sign with an ephemeral P-256 key and upload to the public Rekor log
log a search.sigstore.dev URL during execution
_estate_consequence: The gating means the payload only takes this path inside one upstream repository, so
it will not fire in this estate. What transfers is the technique: any repository here
that combines id-token: write with a publish step can be driven the same way by any
code that reaches its runner. That is a posture question the r5 Actions sweep can
answer, and it is a question the corpus has never asked.

The OIDC trusted-publishing path is the reason to sweep for id-token: write combined with a publish step. That combination is not itself a finding - it is how trusted publishing is supposed to work - but it is the precondition the technique needs, and the sweep has never counted it.
